title: Why Yash's Own Kannada Voice Makes His Ravana Land Harder Than the Hindi Dub
excerpt: Sharad Kelkar voices Ravana for Hindi audiences in Ramayana: Part 1 — and does it well. But critics who have seen both versions say Yash's own pauses and intonation in Kannada are part of the performance no dub can fully recreate.
body:
• In Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part 1 (in cinemas since November 5, in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam), Yash plays Ravana — but Hindi audiences hear Sharad Kelkar's voice, while Yash dubbed his own lines for the Kannada version.
  • Kelkar told Variety India the team chose a Hindi dub because Yash's Kannada-speaking background affects his Hindi accent and rhythm; the decision followed criticism of Yash's Hindi delivery in the trailer.
  • India Today's reviewer argues the Kannada version lands harder — above all in the ten-heads sequence — because Yash's voice, pauses and intonation are part of the performance itself.
  • Choosing a version? Viewers who know Yash from KGF may prefer the Kannada cut (with subtitles where available); the Hindi dub, by the Baahubali voice of Prabhas, is itself drawing praise.

There are two Ravanas in Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana: Part 1, and the difference is a voice. On screen, both belong to Yash, the Kannada superstar cast as the demon king opposite Ranbir Kapoor's Rama and Sai Pallavi's Sita. In the Kannada version, audiences hear Yash himself. In the Hindi version — the film's biggest market — Ravana speaks with the voice of Sharad Kelkar, the dubbing artist known for voicing Prabhas in Baahubali and for his work in Salaar.

The swap was deliberate. Kelkar told Variety India in an exclusive interview that director Nitesh Tiwari and the film's core team decided he should dub for Yash in Hindi, a decision that followed criticism of Yash's Hindi dialogue delivery and pronunciation in the film's trailer. Sai Pallavi's Sita was dubbed for Hindi as well, by Ami Trivedi.

"Yash has given an outstanding performance. He is the best choice for the role and he understood the character perfectly. Dubbing for him was not at all easy."

— Sharad Kelkar, on voicing Ravana in Hindi
https://youtube.com/watch?v=8HiWKbDTc7w

Why the team dubbed — in Kelkar's telling

Kelkar is careful to frame the decision as craft, not correction. Yash speaks Hindi quite well, he said, but as someone who speaks mostly in Kannada, he has an accent, and his rhythm with Hindi words was an issue; the whole team felt the Hindi version needed a dubbed voice. In Kannada, by contrast, "he has done a brilliant job. He has a fantastic voice." Kelkar, who credits his role voicing Lankesh in the animated series The Legend of Hanuman with landing him the part, dubs in sessions of about three hours a day to protect his voice — the session for Ravana's ten-heads sequence ran longer.

The case for the Kannada cut

India Today's Sanjay Ponnappa, reviewing the two versions, argues that something is lost in the exchange. For Yash, he writes, the voice is as much a part of the persona as the attitude and screen presence: in Kannada, the measured pauses, distinct intonation and delivery give the dialogues a rhythm and cultural familiarity that do not feel like a dub struggling to keep the original's weight. The ten-heads sequence is, in his assessment, several times more impactful in Kannada, where shifts in tone track the shades of Ravana. He is equally clear that this is no slight on Kelkar, whose baritone gives the Hindi Ravana considerable weight: "A great dubbing artist can recreate the power of a performance. But sometimes, authenticity is impossible to replicate."

The comparison some viewers are drawing reaches further back: to Dr Rajkumar, the Kannada icon who played Ravana in the 1958 film Bhookailasa. An AI-generated image circulating on X shows Rajkumar handing the legacy of Kannada cinema to Yash — a comparison India Today reads as acknowledgement of a legacy being carried forward rather than an imitation. The difference is less pronounced for Ranbir Kapoor's Rama, whose Kannada dub sits closer to his familiar voice; for Rama, the Hindi original remains the more effective version.

How to watch

Ramayana: Part 1 opened in cinemas on November 5 in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, and its run is still setting records — it has crossed ₹1,000 crore worldwide and posted a record second Friday for a Hindi film. For diaspora audiences choosing between versions, the trade-off is now well documented: the Hindi cut pairs Yash's physical performance with one of India's most accomplished dubbing voices, while the Kannada cut — subtitled in many overseas screenings — is the only one where Ravana sounds like the actor playing him.
